topic: Source Identification & Control — The Undrained Abscess Will Win
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Surgical Unit
speakerBio: An emergency surgeon who has drained more collections than she can count and preaches that the most powerful antibiotic in sepsis is often a scalpel or a drain.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Day 3 of ICU. A 72-year-old man admitted with 'urosepsis' is on the correct antibiotics, adequately filled, and on noradrenaline — yet his lactate will not clear, his fevers keep spiking, and his pressor requirement is creeping up. The overnight team keeps broadening the antibiotics. But antibiotics are not the problem. Somewhere in this man there is a collection, a stone, a device, or a dead piece of tissue that no drug can reach. This session is about finding it and getting rid of it — because the undrained abscess always wins.

1 · The central principle — antibiotics cannot cure a source 🧭

Antibiotics do not cure an undrained abscess, an undebrided necrosis, or an undeviced infection. They hold the line while YOU remove the source.

Antibiotics rely on blood flow to deliver drug to bacteria. The classic septic sources have one thing in common: they are places drug cannot get to in a killing concentration.

Source typeWhy antibiotics failWhat actually cures it
AbscessAvascular pus core, low pH and low oxygen inactivate drug; huge bacterial inoculumDrainage (percutaneous or surgical)
Necrotic / dead tissueNo blood supply = no drug delivery; dead tissue is a bacterial culture mediumDebridement
Infected device / prosthesisBiofilm shields organisms from drug and immune cellsRemoval of the device
Obstructed viscus (biliary, urinary)Stagnant infected fluid under pressure, no drainageDecompression (stent, nephrostomy, ERCP)
💡 One-liner

"Never let the sun set on undrained pus." The septic patient who is not improving on correct antibiotics has a source you have not controlled until proven otherwise.

2 · The mechanism — why a source keeps the fire burning 🔥

A closed infected space is a bacterial fortress:

  1. Huge inoculum: pus contains 10⁸–10⁹ organisms/mL. Even a fully susceptible organism at that density overwhelms drug kinetics (the "inoculum effect").
  2. Poor penetration: the abscess wall is avascular; aminoglycosides are inactivated by the low pH and low oxygen tension inside pus.
  3. Persistent mediator release: as long as live organisms and their toxins sit in the collection, they keep priming the systemic inflammatory response — the shock does not settle.
  4. Ongoing seeding: the source showers the bloodstream, causing relapsing bacteraemia and metastatic infection.

Every hour the source stays in place, the fortress keeps feeding the fire. That is why source control is often more important than the choice of antibiotic.

3 · The systematic hunt — where is it hiding? 🔍

Finding the source is a discipline, not a hunch. Work through history, examination and imaging deliberately.

History & examination

  • History: recent surgery or instrumentation, indwelling lines/catheters, prostheses (joints, valves), immunosuppression, known stones or biliary disease, dental work, intravenous drug use.
  • Examination head-to-toe: every line and every wound looked at and palpated; the abdomen (peritonism, tender gallbladder); flanks (renal angle tenderness); skin and soft tissue (crepitus, pain out of proportion → necrotising fasciitis); a new murmur (endocarditis); perineum and back (never forget the sacral/perianal abscess and epidural collection); joints.

Imaging — match the tool to the question

ModalityBest for
CT (often with contrast)The workhorse — intra-abdominal/pelvic collections, retroperitoneum, chest, occult abscesses. If the patient is 'septic from nowhere,' CT chest/abdo/pelvis is your friend.
UltrasoundRapid bedside look at gallbladder, biliary tree, kidneys/hydronephrosis, ascites, pleural fluid, soft-tissue collections; guides drainage.
EchocardiographyEndocarditis — transthoracic first, but transoesophageal (TOE) is far more sensitive for vegetations, especially prosthetic valves and line-related infection.
MRISpinal/epidural abscess, discitis, soft-tissue and pelvic detail.
🎯 Key concept — the source hunt never stops

A negative first CT does not mean 'no source.' Collections declare themselves over 24–72 hours. If the patient is not improving, re-image — the abscess that was a wisp of fat-stranding on day 1 is a drainable collection on day 3.

4 · Timing — how fast must the source come out? ⏱️

Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021: implement source control as soon as it is logistically and medically feasible after the diagnosis is made — for most sources, aim for within 6–12 hours. Some sources cannot wait even that long.

⚠️ Danger — the sources that cannot wait

Necrotising fasciitis, an obstructed infected kidney, ascending cholangitis, ischaemic/perforated bowel, and infected necrotising pancreatitis with instability are surgical/procedural emergencies measured in hours, not days. In necrotising fasciitis, delay to debridement is one of the strongest predictors of death. Antibiotics buy minutes; the knife or the drain buys survival.

5 · The toolbox — matching the intervention to the source 🧰

SourceSource-control intervention
Intra-abdominal / pelvic abscess, empyemaPercutaneous (image-guided) drainage, or surgery if not amenable
Acute cholecystitis (unfit for surgery)Percutaneous cholecystostomy
Ascending cholangitis / obstructed biliary treeERCP with stone extraction/stenting (or PTC)
Obstructed infected upper urinary tract (stone + pus)Nephrostomy or ureteric stent — decompress urgently
Necrotising soft-tissue infection / fasciitisUrgent surgical debridement, repeated as needed
Infected vascular catheter / line sepsisRemove the line and culture the tip
Infected prosthesis (joint, valve, graft, pacemaker)Device removal/exchange (often staged, with the relevant surgical team)
Perforated viscus / faecal peritonitisLaparotomy, resection/repair, washout
💡 Pearl — least invasive that achieves control

Choose the source-control option with the least physiological insult that will actually work — a percutaneous drain in an unstable patient often beats a big operation. But 'least invasive' must not become 'inadequate': a drain that does not fully evacuate the collection has failed, and the patient needs the definitive procedure.

6 · The undeviced infection — pull the foreign body 🔌

Biofilm is the reason devices must come out. Within hours of colonisation, organisms on a catheter, prosthetic valve, or joint encase themselves in an extracellular polymeric matrix that is ~1000-fold more tolerant of antibiotics and hidden from immune cells. You can suppress a biofilm infection with drugs; you rarely cure it while the device is in.

  • Central line-associated bloodstream infection: remove the line, especially with S. aureus, Candida, Pseudomonas, or persistent bacteraemia.
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis, infected pacemaker/ICD leads, infected joint: hardware removal is usually part of cure — early involvement of cardiology/cardiac surgery, orthopaedics, or vascular surgery.

7 · The patient who does not improve = the missed source 🚩

The septic patient who fails to improve on appropriate antibiotics has a source you have not controlled — until you have proven otherwise.

When your patient is not turning the corner by 48–72 hours, run this checklist before you reflexively broaden the antibiotics:

  1. Is there an undrained collection? → re-image (CT), drain it.
  2. Is there an obstructed viscus (urinary, biliary)? → decompress it.
  3. Is there an infected device or line still in? → pull it.
  4. Is there dead tissue (ischaemic gut, necrotising fasciitis)? → debride it.
  5. Is the drug/dose right and is the bug covered (resistance, fungus)? — only then reconsider the antimicrobials.
☠️ M&M — the 'urosepsis' that was an obstructed, infected kidney

A 74-year-old woman was admitted with fever, flank pain and E. coli in the blood — labelled 'urosepsis,' started on the right antibiotic, filled, and started on noradrenaline. For 48 hours she stayed febrile and pressor-dependent, and each ward round simply broadened her antibiotics. A CT was finally ordered on day 3: a 5 mm ureteric stone with a grossly hydronephrotic, pus-filled kidney above it — a pyonephrosis. That kidney was a closed, obstructed abscess that no intravenous drug could ever sterilise. She went for an emergency nephrostomy that afternoon; frank pus drained, and her shock resolved within hours. Lesson: an obstructed infected urinary tract is a drainage emergency, not an antibiotic problem. 'Urosepsis not improving' means image the kidneys and decompress — the delay, not the bug, nearly killed her.

8 · Take-home 📌

  • Antibiotics hold the line; source control cures. No drug sterilises an undrained abscess, dead tissue, an infected device, or an obstructed viscus.
  • Hunt systematically — history, head-to-toe exam, and targeted imaging (CT workhorse, ultrasound at the bedside, echo/TOE for endocarditis).
  • Timing: source control as early as feasible — aim ≤6–12 h; necrotising fasciitis, obstructed infected kidney and cholangitis are emergencies in hours.
  • Match tool to source: drain, cholecystostomy/ERCP/nephrostomy, debride, remove lines and prostheses, relieve obstruction.
  • Least invasive that fully works — but never mistake inadequate control for control.
  • The septic patient who does not improve has a missed source — re-image before you reflexively broaden the antibiotics.

moderatorQs.q: Why can even a perfectly chosen, fully susceptible antibiotic fail to cure an abscess?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because an abscess is a place the drug cannot work. Pus carries a huge bacterial inoculum (10⁸–10⁹/mL) that overwhelms drug kinetics; the collection is avascular, so drug is not delivered in killing concentrations; and the low pH and low oxygen inside pus inactivate agents such as aminoglycosides. Meanwhile live organisms and toxins keep priming the systemic response, so the shock will not settle until the pus is physically drained. Source control, not the antibiotic, is what cures it.

moderatorQs.q: What is the timing target for source control, and which sources cannot wait for it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: SSC 2021 says implement source control as soon as medically and logistically feasible — for most sources aim within 6–12 hours of diagnosis. But several sources are emergencies measured in hours: necrotising fasciitis (delay to debridement is a major predictor of death), an obstructed infected kidney (pyonephrosis), ascending cholangitis, and perforated/ischaemic bowel. For these, antibiotics only buy minutes — the drain, nephrostomy, ERCP or knife buys survival.

moderatorQs.q: Your septic patient is not improving at 72 hours on correct antibiotics. What is your reasoning?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: My first thought is a missed or uncontrolled source, not the wrong antibiotic. I run a checklist: is there an undrained collection (re-image with CT and drain it), an obstructed viscus — urinary or biliary — to decompress, an infected line or device to remove, or dead tissue to debride? Only after excluding an uncontrolled source do I reconsider the drug, dose, resistance or an unaddressed fungal cause. The patient who fails to improve on appropriate antibiotics has a source I have not yet controlled.

audienceQs.q: For an abscess, when do I choose a percutaneous drain over taking the patient to theatre?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Choose the option with the least physiological insult that will actually achieve control. In an unstable septic patient, an image-guided percutaneous drain often beats a big open operation and can be done under local anaesthesia. Go to theatre when the collection is not amenable to percutaneous drainage (multiloculated, inaccessible, associated with perforation or dead bowel) or when a drain has failed to fully evacuate it. 'Least invasive' must never become 'inadequate' — incomplete drainage is a failed source control.

audienceQs.q: The patient has a central line and keeps growing Staph aureus in blood cultures. Does the line have to come out?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes. Persistent bacteraemia, and specifically Staphylococcus aureus, Candida or Pseudomonas from a line, means the catheter is almost certainly the source and must be removed (and the tip cultured). The reason is biofilm — organisms encased on the catheter are up to ~1000-fold more tolerant of antibiotics and hidden from the immune system, so you cannot reliably sterilise the line in situ. Leaving it in risks relapsing bacteraemia and metastatic seeding such as endocarditis.

audienceQs.q: The first CT was reported as showing no clear collection but the patient is still septic. What do I do?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Do not treat a negative early CT as proof there is no source. Collections declare themselves over 24–72 hours — what was a wisp of fat-stranding on day 1 can be a drainable abscess on day 3. If the patient is not improving, re-image and broaden the search (consider echo/TOE for endocarditis, MRI for spinal/epidural collections, and a look at every line and wound). The source hunt does not stop after one scan.
